questions.stem: This question is about acids, alkalis and indicators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which of these is the colour of litmus indicator in an acidic solution? A blue B orange C red D yellow b) Which of these is the pH value of a neutral solution? A 0 B 4 C 7 D 14

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which of these describes a solution with a pH value of 9? A strongly acidic B strongly alkaline C weakly acidic D weakly alkaline

parts.label: d
parts.text: Which of these is the chemical formula of an acid? A $ \mathrm{H N O_{3}} $ B $ \mathrm{H_{2}O} $ C $ \mathrm{N a C l} $ D $ \mathrm{N a O H} $

parts.label: e

parts.label: f

questions.stem: (a) (i) State the meaning of the term solute. (ii) State the meaning of the term solvent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a saturated solution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A dark purple liquid is diluted by adding water. The diluted liquid becomes a pale purple colour. Explain the process that causes this change. Refer to particles in your answer.

questions.stem: This question is about chromatography. Two students carry out separate chromatography experiments to find the $ R_{f} $ values for five different food dyes, A, B, C, D and E.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two things that should be the same in both experiments so that the students can compare their results fairly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After doing the experiments the students calculate the $ R_{f} $ value for each food dye. The table shows their results.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: State what can be concluded about dye C.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Explain which $ R_{\mathrm{f}} $ value cannot be correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The diagram shows a chromatogram for a different food dye. Some distances are shown on the diagram. Calculate the $ R_{\mathrm{f}} $ value for this food dye. Give your answer to two significant figures.

questions.stem: (a) State the meaning of the term atomic number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An atom of element X contains 14 protons, 14 electrons and 15 neutrons.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Which of these is the mass number of this atom? A 14 B 15 C 28 D 29

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Explain which group of the Periodic Table element X belongs to.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The table shows the composition of a sample of a different element, Y, containing three isotopes. Using information from the table, calculate the relative atomic mass $ ( A_{r} ) $ of this sample of element Y. Give your answer to one decimal place.

questions.stem: This is a question about metals and their compounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one property of metals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Describe the difference in the movement of particles in liquid mercury and in a solid metal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Magnesium is a metal that burns in air.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: State one observation made during the combustion of magnesium metal.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: State one chemical property of the product of combustion that can be used to classify magnesium as a metal.

parts.label: d
parts.text: In the absence of air, magnesium reacts with sulfur to form the ionic compound magnesium sulfide, MgS

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: Give a reason why the reaction needs to be done in the absence of air.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ions in magnesium sulfide. Give the charges on the ions.

parts.label: d-iii
parts.text: Explain why magnesium sulfide has a very high melting point.

parts.label: d-iv
parts.text: Magnesium sulfide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen sulfide gas, $ \mathrm{H_{2} S} $ Give the chemical equation for this reaction.

questions.stem: A student uses this apparatus in an experiment to study the rate of the reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid. This is the student's method. add a few zinc granules to a conical flask on a balance add $ 1 0 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of dilute sulfuric acid to the flask, start a timer and immediately record the mass of the flask and contents record the mass of the flask and contents every minute until the mass remains constant The mass of the flask and contents decreases because hydrogen gas is produced and leaves the flask. The student uses the mass readings to calculate the total mass of hydrogen produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the equation for the reaction by adding the state symbols. $\mathrm {Z n} (\dots \dots \dots \dots) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4} (\dots \dots \dots \dots) \rightarrow \mathrm {Z n S O} _ {4} (\dots \dots \dots \dots) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} (\dots \dots \dots \dots)$

parts.label: b
parts.text: The table shows the student's results.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Plot the student's results. The first three have been done for you.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Draw a circle around the anomalous result.

parts.label: b-iii
parts.text: Draw a curve of best fit.

parts.label: b-iv
parts.text: Give a possible reason for the anomalous result.

parts.label: b-v
parts.text: Determine a more likely value for this result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the shape of the curve shows how the rate of the reaction changes as time increases.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: At the end of the experiment there is no zinc left in the flask. Give a conclusion the student could make from this observation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student does another experiment using the same amount of similarly sized magnesium granules instead of zinc the same volume of sulfuric acid, but of a lower concentration Explain why it is difficult to predict how the rate of reaction in this experiment compares with the rate of reaction in the first experiment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particle collision theory, how increasing the temperature affects the rate of a reaction.

questions.stem: A student is given a mixture of two white solid compounds, and a colourless solution containing the same two compounds. The student is told that one of the compounds is a halide and that the other compound is a carbonate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the student should know, without doing any tests, that one of the compounds cannot be copper(II) carbonate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe tests the student could do to show that the mixture contains potassium carbonate and potassium iodide.

questions.stem: (a) A student is given a pure sample of sodium carbonate crystals and is told that the formula of the crystals is $ \mathrm{N a_{2} C O_{3}. x H_{2} O} $ State what $ x\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} $ in the formula shows about the sodium carbonate crystals.

parts.label: b

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium carbonate left after heating and cooling.

parts.label: b-ii

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student's teacher says that the correct formula of the sodium carbonate crystals is $ \mathrm{N a_{2} C O_{3}. 1 0 H_{2} O} $
